content:
Hi all, I realize I haven't shared complexitylib here before. For context, I am a maintainer of CSLib in the complexity area, and there are a lot of things I want to formalize and experiment with that we are far away from doing yet. To scratch this itch, I've been maintaining complexitylib with several collaborators, an enormous (739,027 lines of Lean in my current checkout) formalization of a menagerie of complexity theorems from the literature: https://github.com/SamuelSchlesinger/complexitylib. Please feel free to contribute if you are a fan of complexity theory.

To give folks a taste of the scope, we prove:

  • Cook–Levin: SAT and 3SAT are NP-complete.
  • The PCP theorem: NP = PCP(O(log n), O(1)), via Dinur’s gap amplification.
  • Cobham’s theorem: a machine-independent function algebra characterizes exactly the polynomial-time computable functions.
  • PSPACE = NPSPACE, via Savitch’s simulation.
  • Sipser–Lautemann: BPP ⊆ Σ₂ᵖ ∩ Π₂ᵖ.
  • Barrington’s theorem: logarithmic-depth Boolean formulas and polynomial-length width-5 permutation branching programs compute the same function families.
  • Håstad’s switching lemma and parity ∉ AC⁰: polynomial-size, constant-depth AND/OR/NOT circuits cannot compute parity.

We also have a few novel results that remain unpublished or from recent preprints. The blueprint links the results to their Lean statements and lays out what remains to be done.

This is all AI maintained and implemented, though there are many ideas of mine and my collaborators in here. We plan to write more details about how we developed this and what we learned at some point. I am slowly working on basing it off of CSLib instead of its own custom foundations, but that is hard and will take some time.

Do you happen to know if the proofs of Barrington's theorem or of parity ∉ AC⁰ were done with the AIs looking at https://github.com/Timeroot/CircuitComp/ at all, which has proofs of both of those (for ~a year now)? For instance your

/-- A single width-`w` branching-program instruction: read variable `var`, and
    apply `perm1` if it is `true`, `perm0` if it is `false`. -/
structure BPInstr (w : ℕ) where
  var : ℕ
  perm0 : Equiv.Perm (Fin w)
  perm1 : Equiv.Perm (Fin w)

abbrev BP (w : ℕ) := List (BPInstr w)

is pretty similar in some regards to

structure GroupProgram (α : Type u) (G : Type v) where
  len : ℕ
  var : Fin len → α
  perm0 : Fin len → G
  perm1 : Fin len → G

although I admit that var, perm0, and perm1 also just perfectly standard-shaped names to just pick. :) (See: #CSLib > Parity is not in AC0 and #CSLib > Formalisation of Barrington's Theorem )

Amusingly, there was also https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24188 posted recently which wrote a paper about formalizing parity ∉ AC⁰!

I'd also like to hear about how some of the design decisions around the Turing-machine parts were made (if those were made by humans). Like, I see that Cook-Levin was done by programming the Turing machine explicitly (first with multi-tape, then single-tape) with a unary encoding ... but for Savitch's theorem you used this nice @[polytime] attribute and used Cobham algebra. Was there a particular reason for the two approaches?

I would just assume the AIs had access to previously existing formalizations and ideally credit those which came first, so I am happy to add any such references. I agree that particular name could have just been a coincidence though!

Re: Turing Machine design decisions, a lot of that was emergent from us trying out different ideas at various points. Also, the AI had very different dexterity levels with Turing Machines at different points in the development, so I had different levels of conviction that any of this would even work. Like, at first it was basically impossible to get the AI to autonomously construct a universal machine without much direction, but now it can do so handily. In work where I am taking on more personal agency, I am trying to migrate to fun_prop (https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Tactic/FunProp.html) style interfaces for proving that programs, represented as Lean functions, are in a particular class by exploiting closure properties, which is that @[polytime] attribute you see. I am slowly figuring out the right way to do that exactly, I just discovered fun_prop a few days ago. My crypto branch on my CSLib fork has a much more substantial use of that idea.
If you are looking through the library, you might get a kick out of some of the circuit work.

That's quite a constant factor! :)
I'll definitely look at how you're doing polytime, I think it seems like a nice approach.
Yes, definitely don't take the particulars of my approach as gospel but I think this kind of approach is going to have legs, especially for usage within reductions.
It is quite nice to imagine essentially having the handwave tactic that we all use when actually showing that X is in polytime :)

I refactored complexitylib to rely entirely on cslib and use better patterns instead of having its own foundations: https://github.com/SamuelSchlesinger/complexitylib2. I am still working on feature parity, but I want to make sure if folks come by here and see complexitylib they know where to find the better version.
Many proofs are dramatically simplified and clarified in the second version.
And the whole codebase is less than a quarter of the size now while retaining most of the significant results.
